frictionVectors.title: EU Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons while supplying Europe through pipelines and LNG. European diversification efforts and price volatility limit Algiers's leverage over time.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's support for the Polisario Front continues to strain relations with Morocco and complicate regional trade, security coordination, and energy integration.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important to Angola's transport and energy networks, creating long-term repayment and strategic-dependence concerns despite efforts to diversify partners.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenue remains central to fiscal stability, leaving sovereign planning vulnerable to production declines, foreign-operator decisions, and global price shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have threatened trade routes and energy ambitions linked to regional infrastructure. Border insecurity also raises costs for northern communities and logistics operators.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's expansion depends on external capital, shipping firms, and regional commerce, creating exposure to foreign commercial leverage and disruptions in neighboring markets.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its negotiating position with major diamond companies, but public revenues remain highly exposed to global demand, synthetic stones, and market concentration.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: A dry climate and limited domestic generation make Botswana reliant on regional power markets and major water infrastructure, constraining full strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Informality
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal and industrial gold production is central to the economy but remains vulnerable to smuggling, armed-group taxation, and opaque off-take networks that weaken state capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced Western influence but creates new risks around accountability, costs, operational effectiveness, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Gold and nickel projects attract foreign capital while weak regulatory capacity and opaque licensing limit Burundi's ability to capture value. Export dependence leaves the state vulnerable to external pricing and financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over rebel support keep the border relationship tense and divert political attention toward security. Regional mediation and aid relationships remain important constraints on independent policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Port and Connectivity Assets
frictionVectors.details: The deep-water port at Mindelo and expanded air and digital links increase Cabo Verde's strategic value to European, Chinese, and U.S. partners. Dependence on external capital creates leverage over infrastructure priorities and debt sustainability.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Burden
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains exposed to transatlantic narcotics trafficking and illegal fishing. Limited naval and surveillance capacity requires sustained outside security assistance, constraining full control of its maritime zone.

highlights: Oil and Timber Value Chains Remain Externalized

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain central to major roads, dams, and other infrastructure, giving Beijing commercial and diplomatic influence. Project financing and implementation can narrow Cameroon's room to prioritize domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Resource Access
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest continues to disrupt transport, agriculture, and local economic control. Security-driven governance and contested access to land and extractive corridors weaken national sovereignty at the periphery.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-for-Resources Model
frictionVectors.details: Russian military advisers and associated commercial networks provide regime protection while seeking influence over gold and diamond activity. This arrangement reduces immediate dependence on some Western partners but risks transferring resource rents and strategic leverage outward.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Mining Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and local power brokers retain influence over mining zones and transport routes outside Bangui. Weak state logistics and insecurity prevent consistent taxation, environmental oversight, and formalization of production.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Sector Externalization
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal position remains heavily dependent on oil produced and marketed through foreign-linked operators and transit infrastructure. Volatile prices and external technical and financial control limit the state's ability to convert reserves into broad-based sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan War Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border political networks from Sudan place sustained pressure on eastern Chad. Security cooperation with foreign partners is expanding, but it also increases outside influence over border and military policy.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to claim Mayotte, while France maintains effective control and treats the island as an overseas department. The dispute constrains bilateral cooperation and fuels domestic political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND FISHERIES DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: External capital and technical assistance remain important for ports, connectivity, and fisheries management. Limited state capacity leaves Comoros vulnerable to unequal deals and weak enforcement of maritime rights.

highlights: Eastern security crisis undermines state control

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACTS AND CRITICAL MINERALS
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt supply chains remain dominated by foreign firms and opaque intermediaries, despite Kinshasa's efforts to renegotiate terms and increase local value addition. Competition among China, Western governments, and Gulf-linked investors raises bargaining leverage but also pressure.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN CORRIDORS AND ARMED GROUPS
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to threaten roads, mining areas, and border trade in the east. Regional rivalries and external security support complicate Kinshasa's ability to consolidate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on offshore oil and foreign technical and financial partners. Production-sharing arrangements and debt obligations limit fiscal room and constrain broader sovereign control over resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: CHINA INFRASTRUCTURE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain central to major roads, public works, and resource-linked infrastructure. These projects improve connectivity but can increase repayment risks and reduce transparency in strategic asset management.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire retains significant influence through sector regulation and farmgate pricing, but foreign processors, traders, and financiers capture much of the value beyond production. Climate stress and farmer incomes remain major vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND EXTERNAL FINANCE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and transport networks attract Chinese, European, Gulf, and regional investment. Competition improves infrastructure, but debt exposure, concession terms, and strategic dependence require careful state oversight.

highlights: Foreign bases trade access for revenue

frictionVectors.title: BASES AND STRATEGIC ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. The arrangement generates revenue and security guarantees but narrows strategic autonomy and increases exposure to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEBT AND CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port and rail infrastructure underpins Ethiopia's trade access but leaves Djibouti exposed to debt, concession, and demand risks. The government retains formal sovereignty while external operators and creditors hold substantial practical leverage.

highlights: Suez and LNG remain strategic revenue anchors

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains Cairo's central sovereignty and food-security concern. Egypt continues diplomatic pressure while avoiding direct escalation.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions and Gulf investment provide essential liquidity but increase foreign influence over major infrastructure, real estate, and logistics assets.

highlights: Mature oil fields weaken fiscal autonomy
Gas monetization is the principal recovery bet

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Decline
frictionVectors.details: Falling crude output and limited diversification leave the state dependent on volatile energy revenues and foreign technical operators.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas and Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: LNG and regional gas projects require external capital and expertise, constraining domestic control over monetization and export infrastructure.

highlights: Red Sea geography raises strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects rely heavily on foreign operators, creating persistent tensions over revenue capture, labor conditions, and regulatory control.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Regional competition around ports and shipping lanes increases outside interest in Eritrean access while limiting Asmara's room for autonomous alignment.

highlights: South African corridors underpin economic resilience
Sugar and forestry remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Imports, energy access, and export routes remain closely tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's independent infrastructure and supply-chain options.

frictionVectors.title: Trade Preference Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, textiles, and forestry depend on external market access and preference regimes, leaving national resource control exposed to foreign regulatory decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD enhances Ethiopia's electricity and bargaining position but continues to generate acute disputes with Egypt and Sudan over filling, drought management, and operating rules.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral financing remains important for transport and energy projects, while debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages constrain sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Belinga and Chinese-linked mining interests
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is seeking greater domestic value capture from iron ore and manganese projects while balancing Chinese capital, contractors, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Trans-Gabon railway vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Rail bottlenecks constrain manganese and timber exports, leaving the state dependent on external operators, financiers, and logistics partners.

frictionVectors.title: Banjul port modernization dependence
frictionVectors.details: The port remains central to Gambian sovereignty and revenue, but expansion depends heavily on foreign finance, contractors, and regional trade flows.

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia security and transport asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies on Senegal for access, security coordination, and overland commerce, limiting independent control of strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and foreign-linked extraction
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage water systems and agricultural land, while foreign-linked supply chains complicate enforcement and domestic value retention.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure financing constraints
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal restructuring and IMF oversight narrow Accra's room to direct resource revenues, while energy and transport projects remain reliant on external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou rail-port consortiums
frictionVectors.details: The corridor could transform Guinea's export capacity, but control is distributed among foreign mining groups, Chinese-backed partners, and infrastructure operators.

frictionVectors.title: Junta-controlled contract environment
frictionVectors.details: Political uncertainty and limited institutional oversight increase the risk that mineral concessions and infrastructure deals favor external actors over transparent national value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cashew value chains
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign buyers, traders, and price shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and maritime security gaps
frictionVectors.details: Weak port capacity and limited naval enforcement create openings for external commercial influence, illicit trafficking, and dependence on foreign security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and heavy exposure to Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders constrain Nairobi's policy space. Public resistance to tax increases and austerity complicates efforts to preserve sovereign control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Northern Corridor Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Competition over Lamu port, the Northern Corridor, and proposed energy infrastructure gives Gulf, Chinese, and regional actors leverage over Kenya's trade architecture. Security threats in northern and coastal areas raise project costs and delay development.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports and hydropower system are structurally tied to South African financing, demand, and infrastructure. This dependence limits Maseru's bargaining power over tariffs, project sequencing, and national resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial and Customs Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The textile and apparel sector remains vulnerable to shifts in United States trade preferences, foreign buyers, and regional customs arrangements. Factory closures or declining orders could sharply reduce employment and fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and rail-to-port infrastructure give foreign mining companies significant influence over export earnings and transport priorities. Liberia's challenge is converting concession revenue into durable domestic capacity rather than renewed enclave growth.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Road Financing
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port, coastal logistics, and major roads depend heavily on external capital and contractors. Competition among Western, Chinese, and regional partners creates leverage but also raises transparency and debt-management concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and production flows. Foreign commercial and diplomatic actors can exploit these divisions to secure preferential access and influence.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenary and Base Networks
frictionVectors.details: External military support, including Turkish and Russian-linked security arrangements, remains embedded in Libya's fragmented security order. Foreign deployments and arms flows constrain unified sovereignty and raise the risk that infrastructure disputes become security crises.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects, especially in nickel and cobalt, are dominated by foreign capital and technology while the state captures only a limited share of downstream value. Commodity-price swings and weak enforcement increase fiscal and environmental vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Port Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Chronic power shortages and limited port capacity leave Madagascar dependent on external financiers and operators for basic economic connectivity. This weakens bargaining power over mining logistics, fuel supply, and future infrastructure concessions.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on IMF and donor financing limit policy autonomy. Foreign-exchange shortages and fuel import dependence remain immediate sovereign-security risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Governance Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in uranium and rare-earth projects, but limited regulatory capacity creates risks of unfavorable terms, weak local value addition, and environmental disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Renegotiation Risk
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pressing foreign mining operators for a larger state share of gold revenues, increasing tensions with established investors while offering limited transparency on contracts and production.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependency Shift
frictionVectors.details: Mali's break with Western partners and reliance on Russian-linked security support have increased geopolitical isolation and may constrain independent control over strategic infrastructure and resource corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project with Senegal offers major fiscal potential but exposes Mauritania to foreign-operator dependence, production delays, and cross-border revenue-management tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Logistics Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports remain dependent on long rail and port corridors vulnerable to financing, maintenance, and buyer concentration risks, particularly involving Chinese demand and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Sovereignty Transition
frictionVectors.details: Greater control over the Chagos maritime space could strengthen Mauritius's sovereign position, but implementation, security arrangements, and relations with external powers remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Import and Connectivity Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutions and diversified services, yet its island economy remains vulnerable to imported energy, food, shipping disruptions, and dependence on external digital infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Contestation
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of territory and associated phosphate, fisheries, and renewable assets continues to face diplomatic and legal challenges, limiting uncontested international investment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Large European, Gulf, Chinese, and other investments are accelerating ports, rail, batteries, and green-hydrogen infrastructure, but may deepen external leverage over strategic supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Control
frictionVectors.details: Major offshore gas projects remain dependent on foreign capital, technology, insurance, and security guarantees. Delays and renegotiations limit Maputo's near-term leverage over export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and External Security
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Delgado insurgency continues to constrain infrastructure and energy development. Rwanda and regional partners provide security assistance, while project operators retain substantial influence over protection arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Finance
frictionVectors.details: New oil, uranium, lithium, and green-hydrogen projects are attracting substantial external investment. Namibia is seeking local processing and fiscal benefits but remains dependent on foreign capital and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, electricity expansion, and export corridors are central to resource plans but require outside financing and regional connectivity. This gives foreign developers and neighboring transit systems leverage over project timing.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating or challenging legacy arrangements with Western-linked mining interests. Efforts to capture more value are constrained by technical, financial, and market dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Reduced Western security cooperation has increased reliance on Russia-linked security support and the Alliance of Sahel States. This expands political autonomy from former partners while creating new dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Capital
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is trying to retain more value through domestic refining and local-content rules, but upstream production still depends heavily on international operators, financing, and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Power Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, pipeline vandalism, and unreliable electricity infrastructure continue to erode state control over resource flows. Private security, distributors, and foreign equipment providers retain significant operational influence.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security and political involvement in eastern Congo keeps it exposed to accusations that regional mineral flows benefit its commercial networks. International scrutiny threatens trade access and diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kigali maintains strong state control over domestic infrastructure and strategic sectors but remains reliant on foreign aid, investment, and security partnerships. Donor pressure can therefore constrain its external and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore licensing and exploration
frictionVectors.details: Potential hydrocarbon blocks attract foreign operators, but limited reserves, financing constraints, and weak state capacity restrict São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago relies on outside partners for maritime surveillance and port-related security, creating influence channels for Portugal, China, and other Gulf of Guinea actors.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production strengthens Dakar's fiscal position, but disputes over contracts, local content, and revenue management test Senegal's ability to convert resources into sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's port and transport corridors face competition from regional hubs and external investors, while infrastructure financing can increase long-term dependence on foreign capital.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime surveillance partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on India, France, and other partners for patrol aircraft, vessels, and maritime-domain awareness, improving security while narrowing strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign investment in scarce land and infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, ports, and coastal development attract external capital, raising concerns over land control, environmental limits, and the concentration of economic influence.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concession politics
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports and public revenue, but concession terms, environmental impacts, and local benefits continue to challenge effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining logistics and port expansion rely heavily on foreign investors and lenders, giving external actors significant influence over strategic infrastructure and export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Port access and security competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Gulf states, and other partners compete for influence over ports, bases, and logistics, often through arrangements involving federal or regional authorities.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource and maritime claims
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas development is constrained by insecurity, overlapping authorities, and maritime disputes, leaving Somalia vulnerable to unfavorable external deals and contested licensing.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transmission Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Improved generation availability has eased rolling blackouts, but Eskom's aging transmission network and municipal debt still constrain reliable sovereign control of the electricity system.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for influence over platinum-group metals, manganese, and other minerals, while South Africa seeks greater domestic processing and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports rely on pipelines and terminals in war-affected Sudan, leaving revenue, maintenance, and transit security vulnerable to external actors and battlefield disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Elite Control of Resource Rents
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and delayed institutional reforms keep oil proceeds concentrated among governing elites, limiting public oversight and weakening national resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Foreign-Backed War Networks
frictionVectors.details: The SAF-RSF conflict is sustained by external political, financial, and military support, leaving ports, trade corridors, and strategic infrastructure divided between rival authorities.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Smuggling and Revenue Loss
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and export channels are contested by armed groups and foreign-linked commercial networks, diverting resource income away from a unified Sudanese state.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Negotiation and Local-Content Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Long-running negotiations over the offshore LNG project reflect Tanzania's effort to secure better fiscal returns, domestic processing, and local participation while managing investor concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Contract Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: The government is tightening oversight of mining and transport corridors, balancing foreign capital needs against demands for greater state revenue, processing, and environmental control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a regional gateway attracts foreign logistics and security interests, but dependence on external capital and volatile Sahel trade routes limits fully autonomous infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate Value-Chain Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources, yet limited domestic processing and financing leave substantial value capture exposed to foreign buyers, technology providers, and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation remain closely linked, giving Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance to perceived external conditionality complicates implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Imported energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported gas and electricity, particularly through dependence on Algeria and volatile international prices. Renewable projects are advancing but have not yet materially restored energy sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's resource strategy but faces sustained criticism, financing constraints, and reputational pressure from Western governments and civil-society groups. Chinese and Gulf-linked capital could become more important as Western participation narrows.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability around eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and persistent militant threats raise costs for transport corridors and extractive projects. Uganda's security role provides influence but also increases external scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: Competition over copper assets
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using renewed copper demand to renegotiate value capture and attract competing investors from China, the United States, the Gulf, and Europe. Concentration of refining, logistics, and technology outside Zambia still limits full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and power bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on regional rail, ports, and electricity imports exposes copper exports to infrastructure and drought-related shocks. New Lobito and alternative corridor investments improve bargaining power but remain incomplete.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is tightening controls on unprocessed lithium and other minerals, but Chinese firms retain a strong position in mining, processing, and market access. The state has increased leverage without yet securing broad domestic beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Financial isolation and infrastructure gaps
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and limited access to conventional finance push Harare toward non-Western lenders and opaque bilateral arrangements. Electricity shortages, transport constraints, and currency instability continue to weaken domestic resource capture.
